title: Catalogue and Gaia DR3 values rank 2020-2026 TFOP verdicts on TESS candidates with AUC 0.90-0.96, but models fit on early verdicts predict too few planets because false positives get verdicts first
abstract: Question: Can catalogue values and Gaia DR3 data that exist before follow-up predict which TESS Objects of Interest (TOIs) become planets, and are the probabilities correct for later verdicts? Method: We combined TOI-table values with Gaia DR3 host and neighbour data (RUWE, RV-variability flag, neighbours that can make the transit depth, eclipsing-binary period matches) in gradient-boosted and logistic models. We did forward tests with archived TOI tables of 2020-11-20 and 2021-05-06 against TFOPWG verdicts of 2026-11-09. Results: For 739 candidates open in 2020 and resolved by 2026, 2020 inputs rank the verdicts with cross-validated AUC 0.96 (catalogue only 0.94, Gaia only 0.88). Models trained only on the verdicts known in 2020 or 2021 keep AUC 0.90-0.92 but predict 0.17-0.33 planets where 0.57-0.59 occurred (logistic intercept error +3.1). The cause is verdict timing: the planet fraction was 8.5% for verdicts given by 2020-11-20, 41% for verdicts in the next six months and 62% for verdicts after 2021-05-06. A 2026 model on 2,238 resolved candidates has AUC 0.95 when each alert year is held out, and its mean prediction matches the observed planet fraction. It predicts 1,555 (bootstrap 1,410-1,630) planets among 5,323 open candidates, with probability 0.79 below 1.5 Earth radii and 0.06 above 16. An outcome-independent Gaia RV check finds 351 RV-variable hosts where 379 +- 16 were expected; this limits the remaining base-rate bias to about +0.2 log-odds for bright hosts. Archived 2020 TOI ephemerides have correct core uncertainties but 11% are off by more than 3 sigma in 2026. Limitations: verdicts are not ground truth; faint-star candidates are poorly represented among verdicts, and the RV check covers only hosts with G_RVS <= 12; no light-curve data were used.

citations.reason: We use its Gaia DR3 eclipsing-binary period-match method as one model input and confirm that such matches occur for false positives and not for planets.
We use the Katz et al. RV-variability flag in the same way, and use it as an outcome-independent check of open-candidate reliability.
We reuse its copy of the TRICERATOPS 2021 table and compare TRICERATOPS FPP with our model on the same TOIs.
Its heavy-tailed CTOI timing errors also occur for archived TOI ephemerides.
Its catalogue period errors agree with the heavy tails we find in 2020-to-2026 TOI ephemeris changes.
It bounds missing-verdict effects; we measure the verdict-timing effect directly with three table snapshots.
